Federated Learning for Internet of Things:
Applications, Challenges, and Opportunities
Tuo Zhang, Lei Gao, Chaoyang He, Mi Zhang, Bhaskar Krishnamachari, Salman Avestimehr
Abstract—Billions of IoT devices will be deployed in the near
future, taking advantage of the faster Internet speed and the
possibility of orders of magnitude more endpoints brought by
5G/6G. With the blooming of IoT devices, vast quantities of data
that may contain private information of users will be generated.
The high communication and storage costs, mixed with privacy
concerns, will increasingly be challenging the traditional ecosys-
tem of centralized over-the-cloud learning and processing for IoT
platforms. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as the most
promising alternative approach to this problem. In FL, training
of data-driven machine learning models is an act of collaboration
between multiple clients without requiring the data to be brought
to a central point, hence alleviating communication and storag

e
costs and providing a great degree of user-level privacy. We
discuss the opportunities and challenges of FL for IoT platforms,
as well as how it can enable future IoT applications.
Index Terms —Federated Learning, IoT, Privacy-preserving
Machine Learning
I. I NTRODUCTION
Recently, Facebook has changed its company name to
Meta as it shifts its focus to the metaverse, the universe of
virtual worlds that are all interconnected [1]. That brings the
collaborative and active learning for the Internet of Things
(IoT) back to the spotlight, as a massive number of IoT devices
will be deployed to develop an ecosystem that will eventually
evolve into the metaverse. However, the fast expansion of IoT
networks poses new challenges to the traditional centralized
over-the-cloud approaches for data analysis as IoT devices
are generating an unprecedented amount of data [2]. On the
one hand, centralized approaches no longer ﬁt the 5G/6G
era due to the extremely high communication and storage
overhead

(e.g., high-frequency data from high-volume time-
series sensors such as video cameras or Lidar sensors) for
pooling data from many IoT devices. Cisco has estimated that
nearly 850 ZB of data will be generated by all the people,
machines, and things on the network edge by the end of
2021 [3], but annual global data center IP trafﬁc will only
reach 20.6 ZB in this year. On the other hand, the data
being collected is increasingly viewed as threatening user
privacy. With the centralized over-the-cloud approaches, user
data will be shared between or even sold to various companies,
violating privacy rights and negatively affecting data security,
further driving public distrust with data-driven applications.
Therefore, an innovative data management approach for data-
driven learning and inference-based applications is needed for
efﬁciency and to alleviate privacy concerns.
Federated learning (FL), a nascent ﬁeld, has been proposed
as a distributed privacy-preserving solution to addressing th

is
pressing need [4]. In FL, training of the machine learning
Fig. 1: Federated Learning for IoT Devices.
models needed for data-driven applications is an act of collabo-
ration between multiple clients without centralizing the data of
the clients so as to preserve user privacy. The distributed nature
of FL is a good match to the IoT network where each edge
device in the IoT network is an individual client. Since the raw
data of each device will not be exposed to others, FL is an
effective way to address the above challenges, particularly in
the IoT domain, where the sensors may directly sense or infer
data about users that contains sensitive personal information.
In this article, we explain the advantages that FL brings to
the IoT domain. We will also discuss some of the most impor-
tant IoT applications enabled by these advantages. Lastly, we
will discuss some of the outstanding challenges when applying
FL to IoT applications, and the opportunities in tackling these
challenges. We ho

pe this article can act as an enabler to inspire
new research at the intersection of federated learning and IoT.
II. W HY FEDERATED LEARNING FOR IOT?
The term federated learning was ﬁrst introduced in 2016 by
McMahan et al. [5]. As shown in Figure 1, FL is a framework
for collaborative training of global machine learning models
from multiple datasets that are distributed over separate clients,
whereas the datasets are not shared among clients during the
training phase. There are generally two main roles inside
an FL framework: clients holding their own datasets for the
training, and the server that arranges the entire training process
and generates the global model without accessing any local
datasets. During the FL training, the server ﬁrst initializes the
model weights and hyperparameters and distributes the model
to individual clients. After receiving the model information
sent by the server, each client starts to train the model using
its local dataset and then sends its updated lo

cal information,

2
Fig. 2: Advantages of Federated Learning for IoT Devices.
such as the model weights or the gradients, to the server
for model aggregation. FedAvg is one of the most popular
aggregation functions [6], which generates the global model
by equally averaging weights or gradients of each model. After
model aggregation, the server distributes the global model to
all clients for the next round of training.
The privacy-preserving, collaborative, and distributed nature
of FL brings a number of key advantages for IoT applications
(Figure 2) as follows:
 Preserving the Privacy of User Data : In an ideal FL
scenario, each IoT device in the system would learn
nothing more than the information needed to play their
role. The raw data never leaves the devices during the
process and only the updates of the model will be sent to
the central server, which minimizes the risk of personal
data leakage.
 Improving Model Performance: Due to device c

onstraint,
single IoT devices may not have sufﬁcient data to learn a
high-quality model by itself. Under the FL framework,
all the IoT devices can collaboratively train a high-
quality model such that each participant could beneﬁt
from learning data collected by others beyond its own
data. Thus, FL is an effective mechanism to enhance the
model performance that each individual device cannot
achieve by itself.
 Flexible Scalability: The distributed nature of FL is able
to leverage the constrained computation resources located
at multiple IoT devices across different geographical
locations in a parallel manner. By attracting more de-
vices to join the framework, FL enhances the scalability
of IoT networks without adding an extra burden on a
centralized server due to its distributed learning nature.
In addition, within the FL framework, there is no need for
the expansive transmission of the raw IoT-collected data.
Instead, the communication to the server will mainly be
focused on the mod

el updates, which also increases the
scalability with regard to communication costs, especially
for the low bandwidth IoT networks.
III. K ILLER APPLICATIONS
Enabled by the advantages mentioned above, FL has enabled
many important IoT applications. In this section, we discuss
some of the most important ones (Figure 3).
A. Healthcare
As IoT devices become more pervasive in individuals’ daily
lives, the privacy of the collected data becomes a signiﬁcant
matter. An example to illustrate privacy concerns is IoT E-
health. Nowadays, smart wearable devices are used to monitor
the health status of patients such as heartbeat, blood pressure,
and glucose level. Compared to the other types of data,
personal healthcare data is most sensitive to privacy and highly
restricted to the government regulation for any kinds of data
sharing [7]. To moderate the above challenges, FADL [8]
ﬁrst proposes a federated training framework that allows each
hospital to participate in learning part of the model usi

ng its
own medical data source. Yuan et al. [9] presents a similar co-
operative healthcare framework enabled by FL among medical
IoT devices. Very recently, the potential of FL has also been
discovered during the ﬁght with the COVID-19 pandemic. Liu
et al. [10] brings an FL-based system that allows hospitals
to cooperate in training the models for identifying CT scans
of COVID-19 patients without transmitting raw data, which
breaks the data isolation problem for IoT E-health.
B. Cybersecurity
With the expansion of the IoT networks, the potential trafﬁc
volume of IoT-based DDoS attacks is reaching unprecedented
levels, as witnessed during the Mirai botnet attack leveraging
infected webcams and home routers [11]. Attacks such as this
have raised awareness of the need for IIoT risk assessment
and security, e.g. in ﬁelds such as healthcare. FL can offer
an alternative approach for IoT cybersecurity by protecting
the network from malicious attacks as close as possible to
the edge devices.

DIoT [12] is the ﬁrst system to employ an
FL approach to anomaly-detection-based intrusion detection in
gateways to IoT devices. IoTDefender [13] is another similar
framework, which obtains personalized models on each local
device by ﬁne-tuning the global model trained with FL to ﬁlter
the malicious trafﬁc. Recently, the FedML Ecosystem [14]–
[18] proposes the ﬁrst FL platform designed speciﬁcally for
IoT devices and the FedDetect algorithm to catch anomalous
trafﬁc. Their experiments on the Raspberry Pi demonstrate the
efﬁciency and feasibility of deploying FL on IoT devices.
C. Smart Home
Smart home systems enabled by consumer IoT devices have
achieved great popularity in the last few years as they improve
the comfort and quality of life for the residents [19]. The
wireless smart IoT home devices, such as smart bulbs, smart
doorbells, and smart cameras, are capable of communicating
with each other and controlled remotely by smartphones
and microcontrollers. People now tend to rely on

smart IoT
gateways like Amazon Alexa and Apple HomePod to control
the house hands-free. While enjoying the convenience brought
3
Fig. 3: Applications of Federated Learning for IoT Devices.
by these IoT devices, we could not ignore the essence of
privacy-preserving, especially in our own homes. For example,
the leakage of the personal voice data for the voice control
gives hackers an opportunity to create the imitation. Many
works have implemented the FL to address the above chal-
lenge. Researchers from Apple have proposed a federated
learning model with differential privacy to improve the on-
device speaker veriﬁcation while reducing the risk of raw data
leakage [20]. Also, SecWIR [21] is proposed as a framework
for securing the smart home IoT communications via Wi-Fi
routers.
D. Smart City
IoT-enabled smart cities are bringing signiﬁcant advance-
ments by making city operations efﬁcient while improving the
quality of life for citizens [22]. Various IoT devices enable
city managers t

o control the physical objects in real-time
and provide intelligent information to citizens in terms of
the trafﬁc system, transportation, public safety, healthcare,
smart parking, and smart agriculture, and so on. For example,
some researchers propose a dynamic dispatcher for a ﬂeet of
electric buses based on the real-time trafﬁc and weather data
[23]. Due to the concerns of data privacy, smart infrastruc-
tures are moving to compute resources close to where data
reside, which makes FL framework suitable for deployment.
Distream [24] represents the ﬁrst distributed framework that
enables workload-adaptive live video analytics under the smart
camera-edge cluster architecture, which represents a step to-
wards turning the envisioned large-scale live video analytics
with privacy-preserving into reality.
E. Industry 4.0
The rapid development in the Industrial Internet of Things
(IIoT) brings several advances in information technology ap-
plications for the manufacturing ﬁeld. The concept

of Industry
4.0, also known as the fourth industrial revolution, has been
proposed based on the emergence of signiﬁcance for the
inter-connectivity based on IIoT and the access to real-time
data [25]. With unprecedented connectivity, Industry 4.0 will
bring greater insight, control, and data visibility for the supply
chain in many industries. However, there are still some real-
world problems challenging the deployment of Industry 4.0.
First, the amount of data generated from a single factory
may not be sufﬁcient enough for training a reliable model
comprehensively. Second, the data collected by the IIoT de-
vices is highly related to the commercial value, which makes
privacy-preserving important. For example, eavesdroppers may
infer the capacity for manufacture from its electricity usage
for industrial IoT users. To address the above challenges,
Lu et al. [26] proposed a blockchain and FL-based data-
sharing framework in IIoT. Its empirical results demonstrate
the efﬁciency of FL usag

e in IIoT.
F . Autonomous Driving
Along with the advancement of the Vehicular IoT, au-
tonomous driving system is gradually getting close to the
ordinary living. For a reliable self-driving system, it needs
frequent real-time communication with multi-access commu-
nication environment. Also, the spatial and temporal changes
of vehicular environment require an intelligent approach that
can evolve with the change of environment. For the traditional
centralized-over-cloud method, the driving system need to
transmit large amount of raw data to the server, which would
cause potential privacy leakage. The communication delay
triggered the large-size data transmission may also let the driv-
ing system could not respond to the real-time spatial changes
for the vehicle movement precisely. Using federated learning
based on vehicular edge computing for autonomous driving
will become a promising direction to mitigate the above
challenges. Within FL, each vehicle only needs to transmit a
limited si

ze data to the cloud. Also, FL could make the vehicle
adopt to real-time local changes more sensitively. In [27], the
authors proposed a blockchain-supported federated learning
for trustworthy vehicular networks. Within their network, each
vehicle will use FL framework to generate a global decentral-
ized model. For the critical cars like police cars or ﬁre cars,
the weights will go through the blockchain before to the server
to authenticate they are true and authentic. Their simulation
results demonstrate that FL could ensure trustworthiness and
adherence to delay requirements for vehicles in VNet systems.
G. Metaverse and Virtual Reality
The metaverse is a hypothesized next generation of the
internet, providing fully connected, immersive and engaging
online 3D virtual experiences through conventional personal
computing, as well as virtual and augmented reality devices
[28]. In metaverse, users own their avatars and assets and
can collaborate and interact with virtual objects and othe

r
participants. Metaverse could provide a new platform for
business, socialization, entertainment, education, manufacture,
and etc. The process towards building the metaverse will
require further development of multiple emerging technologies
including AI, IoT, AR/VR, edge/cloud compute, blockchain
and 5G. To establish the convergence between physical and
virtual world, it is essential to create the digital twins of the
real objects, environments and assets. By processing data from
IoT devices, digital twins could not only replicate the physical
appearance and also reﬂect the real time information such
performance and status changes from the physical world. Due
to the increasing amount of collected data and data privacy
concerns, FL as a distributed collaborative AI approach could
further enhance the role of IoT in metaverse scenarios by
leveraging the advantages mentioned in section II.

IV. C HALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES
To realize the full potential of FL in the applications men-
tio

ned above, there still exist several fundamental challenges
that need to be addressed. In this section, we describe eight
research challenges followed by opportunities that have high
promise to address those challenges.
A. Limited Computational Resources
The deployment of FL on IoT networks highly relies on
the memory and computational resources at edge devices.
However, people often only focus on the ability of IoT
devices to collect data, and disregard their limited memory and
computational resources, which make it difﬁcult for most IoT
devices to ﬁnish local computation with large data or complex
models [29].
To address this challenge, it is critical to explore lightweight
AI algorithms that can be implemented in the resource-
constrained FL-IoT environment, as well as optimized re-
source management methods to facilitate on-device FL train-
ing. FedGKT [30] reformulated FL as a group knowledge
transfer training algorithm for the large-size model training on
resource-constrained edg

e devices. Facemask [31] is recently
proposed as a joint computation and communication-efﬁcient
personalized FL framework via heterogeneous masking. In
particular, FedMask could improve the communication cost
and the computation cost by 34.48x and 2.44x respectively
compared to the personalized fedavg framework, which serves
as a critical step to mitigate this challenge.
B. Device Heterogeneity
Within cross-device settings, participants under the FL
framework have diverse system resources, such as computation
and memory resources. As the trend in machine learning is for
larger and deeper models, the hardware heterogeneity inside
the IoT system poses a challenge for the federated learning
framework. As the devices with powerful computation and
memory resources, they could train the large models easily
while the other devices could only train the smaller models
with limited resources. Even for the same model size, the
training speed will vary across devices, which may trigger the
asynchr

onous communication problem as we addressed above.
An FL framework for IoT should enable graceful adaptation
of the data and compute load across different devices based
their on their resource availability.
C. Limited Networking Bandwidth
Communication overhead is considered one of the major
challenges in an FL-based IoT environment. Currently, most
of IoT devices communicate using wireless networks whose
bandwidth is much less than wired network bandwidth. As the
more devices joining into the system, the communication prob-
lem is advent when clients possess with different resources
allocations. The limited network bandwidth not only makes the
communication between clients and server inefﬁcient, but also
triggers the presence of straggler clients, which fail to share its
local update with the server during the communication round.
Fig. 4: Challenges of Federated Learning for IoT Devices.
They both serve as the bottlenecks for the performance of FL
deployment in the large-scale IoT sce

nario.
To address this challenge, some key ideas have been pro-
posed in the past few years, such as decentralized training,
data compression and participant selections. Mercury [32]
recently proposed a sampling-based framework that enables
efﬁcient on-device distributed training without compromising
the training quality as a new inspiration for solving this
challenge.
D. Asynchronous Communication
Currently, most of the FL studies are based on the syn-
chronous update at the server, which means that the server
will not start the model aggregation until it receives the
information sent from the slowest edge device. However, due
to the unbalanced communication abilities and training data
distribution, the local training speed varies from device to
device, even some participants will temporarily drop off during
the training phase, which makes the synchronous update nearly
impossible. In the asynchronous FL scenarios, a client could
join the active learning group even in the middle of the

training
progress, which endangers the convergence of the algorithm.
To address this challenge, some researchers proposed asyn-
chronous aggregation scheme with the implementation of
coding theory to resist the stragglers in the FL system. In
[33], an asynchronous aggregation protocol known as FedBuff
has been proposed to mitigate stragglers and enable secure
aggregation jointly. Speciﬁcally, the individual updates are not
incorporated by the server as soon they arrive. Instead, the
server will keep receiving local updates in a secure buffer of
size K, which is a tunable parameter, and then update the
global model when the buffer is full. To extend the limit
of buffer size K, [34] is proposed to mitigate the memory
limitation for buffered asynchronous aggregation.
E. Data Heterogeneity
In IoT settings, the data collected by different devices can
be very different in their characteristics, and various types of
devices have different preferences for their data collection,
which may crea

te a discrepancy in the local data structure
among all the participants in FL. For example, a surveillance
5
camera will record in real-time (24x7 hours), while the data
generated by a doorbell is intermittent. However, the central
server could not examine the impact of the data heterogeneity
until the training is over.
To address this challenge, we envision that the training
quality and speed will be improved if we could determine the
heterogeneity and make adjustments accordingly before the
training starts. Another popular direction for this challenge
is to reduce the model bias via efﬁcient regulations for the
training.
F . Device Dropout and Participant Selection
Due to the heterogeneity of data collected and the diversity
of IoT devices along with their deployment settings, not every
IoT device could effectively contribute to the global model
under the FL framework. Especially under large-scale IoT
systems, millions of devices will be operated under the same
network. Not all of th

em will be simultaneously available for
FL updating. Also, their heterogeneous data distribution may
lead to a sub-optimal ﬁnal result.
To address this challenge, Oort [35] is proposed as a
guided participant selection algorithm to address the above
challenge. Oort enforces the requirements on the distribution
of participant data while improving the duration of federated
testing by cherry-picking clients to improve the overall training
efﬁciency.
G. Lifelong/Continual Learning
IoT sensing devices will, by their very nature, continuously
collect new data, which will be used to update the model
for lifelong or continual learning. While keep providing cus-
tomized services, the continued model update training poses
a new challenge for resource-limited IoT devices. On one
hand, as most of the edge devices are memory-limited, their
computation resources are not sufﬁcient enough to handle both
model inference and training. On the other hand, the energy-
constrained nature of IoT devices also

makes edge devices
could not distribute sufﬁcient resources for the efﬁcient con-
tinue learning process. Furthermore, lack of sufﬁcient memory
to keep past collected data, may accelerate catastrophic for-
getting [36] in continual FL.
To address this challenge, we envision that the light-
weighted machine learning engine is needed to reduce the
memory consumption for on-device training. For example,
FedGKT [30], MEST [37], and TinyFL [38] are potential
methods to reduce the training memory footprint for efﬁcient
on-device learning. To avoid catastrophic forgetting we also
envision the use of clustering approaches that identify and
store few core datasets from each time interval or leveraging
IoT “Hubs” that can store non-sensitive/public datasets to in-
ject memory in the training system. Approaches that can detect
temporal distribution shifts at each IoT node to determine
when to update the model would also be needed.
H. Adversarial Attack and Defense
In the real-world deployment, t

he prevalence of the IoT de-
vices also poses an attractive target for adversaries seeking to
launch attacks, such as phishing, identity theft, and distributed
denial of service (DDoS). Even though these attacks could
be easily defended by installing security patches, many IoT
devices lack the requisite computation resources to do so. It is
crucial for the IoT system to detect the malicious or broken IoT
devices that will ruin the model training with limited resource.
To address this challenge, one of the promising directions
is to implement a lightweight security protocol in the IoT
system for the detection of broken and malicious devices.
For example, SecWIR [21] is proposed as a framework for
securing the smart IoT communications via Wi-Fi routers with
embedded intelligence for the home-based IoT system.
V. C ONCLUDING REMARKS
Federated learning has become an important privacy-
preserving for machine learning paradigm. Its distributed na-
ture makes it well suited for deployment in

many Internet of
Things applications. In this article, we have summarized the
advantages and elaborated on some important applications of
federated learning for IoT. We have also identiﬁed and detailed
some key research challenges for the future development of FL
on IoT. We hope this article could attract more attention to the
federated learning ﬁeld and inspire creativity and innovation
needed to build the FL-IoT ecosystem.
